scenes.head: Receivables and payables
scenes.sub: Selling on credit creates receivables, and some of them will never be paid. Learn the allowance method that US GAAP and IFRS require, estimate bad debts by aging and by a percentage of sales, account for notes receivable, and build up a business’s current liabilities, using Lantern’s first year-end.

segs.say: Receivables and payables. Selling on credit creates receivables, and some of them will never be paid. Learn the allowance method that US GAAP and IFRS require, estimate bad debts by aging and by a percentage of sales, account for notes receivable, and build up a business’s current liabilities, using Lantern’s first year-end.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Explain why US GAAP and IFRS require the allowance method for receivables, what the CECL model (ASC 326) asks for, and why the direct write-off method is acceptable only for immaterial amounts.
Calculate the allowance for doubtful accounts by aging receivables and by a percentage of credit sales, and the bad debt expense when the allowance has a credit or a debit balance before adjustment.
Record credit sales, collections, write-offs, recoveries and the year-end bad debt adjustment, and report receivables net of the allowance.
Calculate the interest on a note receivable and record its accrual and collection.
Identify and measure a business’s current liabilities (accounts payable, accrued liabilities, unearned revenue and income taxes payable) and assemble them for the balance sheet.

scenes.head: Lantern’s online shop is paid by card when each order is placed, so it never waits for its money.

segs.say: Lantern’s online shop is paid by card when each order is placed, so it never waits for its money. Catering is different. Apart from Harbor Tech’s prepaid events, Lantern invoiced its catering clients $59,920 during the year on 30-day terms, and by 31 December it had collected $51,720. One client, Quayline Events, closed down in November owing $820 for a September event, and Lantern wrote the invoice off. The other $7,380 is still owed: some of it will arrive in January, and some of it, almost certainly, never will.

scenes.head: When a business delivers goods or services and lets the customer pay later, it holds accounts receivable: the customer’s obligation to pay, usually…

segs.say: When a business delivers goods or services and lets the customer pay later, it holds accounts receivable: the customer’s obligation to pay, usually within 30 to 60 days and without interest. Under IFRS they are called trade receivables. Each invoice states the credit terms. Lantern’s “n/30” means the full (net) amount is due within 30 days; “2/10, n/30” would offer 2% off to a client who pays within 10 days. Discounts for prompt payment (sales discounts) reduce revenue and are covered in the revenue recognition lesson; this lesson is about what happens after the invoice is sent.

scenes.head: Businesses sell on credit because customers expect it.

segs.say: Businesses sell on credit because customers expect it. Corporate clients, hotels and event agencies pay suppliers by invoice, and a caterer that demanded cash in advance from all of them would lose work. The price of credit is that some customers pay late and a few never pay. That raises two accounting questions: when should the loss from customers who won’t pay be recognised as an expense, and at what amount should the receivables be shown on the balance sheet?

scenes.head: Both questions have the same answer, the allowance method.

segs.say: Both questions have the same answer, the allowance method. At the end of each period the business estimates how much of its receivables it does not expect to collect, records that amount as bad debt expense in the period of the sales, and holds it in the allowance for doubtful accounts, a contra account deducted from Accounts Receivable. The difference, net receivables, is the amount the business expects to collect. When a particular customer later proves unable to pay, the account is written off against the allowance, with no new expense, because the loss was already expected and recorded.
Where Lantern’s catering invoices went in 2026, and how the year-end estimate divides what is still owed (fictional figures in dollars; bar lengths to scale within each bar).

scenes.head: Lantern’s year-end shows the method at work.

segs.say: Lantern’s year-end shows the method at work. The $820 owed by Quayline is gone: there is no point listing it as an asset. Of the $7,380 still owed, Lantern’s accountant expects $584 not to be collected, so the balance sheet shows receivables of $7,380 less an allowance of $584, net $6,796. The year’s bad debt expense covers both losses, the $820 already known and the $584 expected, which is why the adjusting entry is for $1,404. The rest of this lesson explains each step, then turns to the other side of the balance sheet: what Lantern owes.

scenes.head: Two events, two entries

segs.say: Two events, two entries. The estimate at the period end is the expense: debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. The write-off of a named customer is not an expense: debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, credit Accounts Receivable. Keeping them apart puts the loss in the period of the sale, whenever the customer is finally given up on.

scenes.head: Payables are the mirror image.

segs.say: Payables are the mirror image. Lantern buys beans from Kilnworth Roasting on 30-day terms, owes its staff for the last days of December, owes interest on two notes, holds customers’ money for services it has not yet delivered, and owes income tax for the year. Each is a current liability, and each is measured differently. Together they tell a lender, and Ana, how much cash Lantern must find in the next few months.

scenes.head: Accounts Receivable is a control account: behind it sits a subsidiary ledger with one account for each client, so that Lantern knows who owes what…

segs.say: Accounts Receivable is a control account: behind it sits a subsidiary ledger with one account for each client, so that Lantern knows who owes what and since when. The balance moves in a simple pattern, which the formula card calls the receivables roll-forward: what was owed at the start, plus credit sales, minus collections, minus write-offs. Lantern began in March with nothing owed, so its year is 0 + 59,920 − 51,720 − 820 = 7,380. A business that knows three of the four movements can always find the fourth, a quick reasonableness check that auditors use on collections.
Lantern’s receivables accounts for 2026 (fictional): y8 invoices, y9 collections, y10 the Quayline write-off, e6 the year-end estimate

chapters.title: Why the direct write-off method is not enough

scenes.head: The simplest approach, the direct write-off method, records nothing until a particular customer is known not to pay, and then debits Bad Debt Expense…

segs.say: The simplest approach, the direct write-off method, records nothing until a particular customer is known not to pay, and then debits Bad Debt Expense and credits Accounts Receivable. Small businesses that keep their books for tax often work this way. It fails as financial reporting for two reasons. The expense lands in the period when the customer gives up, which is often a later year than the sale that earned the revenue. And until then the balance sheet shows receivables at the full amount owed, although some of that amount is not expected to be collected.

scenes.head: For these reasons US GAAP and IFRS require receivables to be measured net of expected losses, which means an allowance.

segs.say: For these reasons US GAAP and IFRS require receivables to be measured net of expected losses, which means an allowance. The direct write-off method survives only where bad debts are immaterial: the Codification itself says that its provisions need not be applied to immaterial items (ASC 105-10-05-6), so a business whose losses are trivially small may expense them when they occur. Tax rules are different. The IRS lets a business deduct a bad debt when it becomes wholly or partly worthless, so the tax deduction follows the write-off, not the estimate, and a company’s books and tax return will show different bad debt figures for the same year.

chapters.title: The allowance method, entry by entry

scenes.head: Three kinds of entry run through the allowance account.

segs.say: Three kinds of entry run through the allowance account. The estimate is an adjusting entry at the period end: debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. The write-off of a named customer removes the balance from both the subsidiary ledger and the control account: debit the allowance, credit Accounts Receivable. A recovery, when a customer who was written off later pays after all, is recorded in two steps: first reverse the write-off for the amount recovered (debit Accounts Receivable, credit the allowance), then record the cash received (debit Cash, credit Accounts Receivable). Reinstating the receivable first keeps the customer’s history complete, so the credit file shows that the customer did pay.
Lantern’s write-off and year-end estimate, and a recovery in 2027 (y10 and e6 are from the case; the recovery is hypothetical)

scenes.head: In a business that keeps its allowance up to date, a write-off changes neither total assets nor net receivables: receivables and the allowance fall…

segs.say: In a business that keeps its allowance up to date, a write-off changes neither total assets nor net receivables: receivables and the allowance fall by the same amount. With receivables of $10,000 and an allowance of $900, net receivables are $9,100; writing off $820 leaves $9,180 less $80, still $9,100. Lantern’s position was different: it prepares annual statements and made its first estimate only at 31 December, so when Quayline was written off in November there was nothing in the allowance to absorb it. The account went into a debit balance of $820, which means only that a loss happened before any had been expected. The year-end adjustment must cover that loss as well as building the $584 needed for the receivables still held.

scenes.head: There are two ways to arrive at the estimate.

segs.say: There are two ways to arrive at the estimate. The income statement approach applies a loss rate to the period’s credit sales and records that amount as the expense; whatever is left in the allowance afterwards is the balance. The balance sheet approach starts from the receivables still held at the period end, decides how large the allowance must be, and records whatever expense brings the account to that balance. Its most common form is an aging of receivables, which sorts each customer’s balance by how long it has been outstanding and applies a higher loss rate to older balances, because the longer an invoice is overdue the less likely it is to be paid.
Lantern Coffee Co.: aging of receivables at 31 December 2026 (fictional)

scenes.head: The aging says that $584 of the $7,380 should be held as an allowance.

segs.say: The aging says that $584 of the $7,380 should be held as an allowance. Before the adjustment the allowance has a debit balance of $820, so the entry must first bring it back to zero and then build the $584 credit: bad debt expense is 584 + 820 = 1,404 (adjustment e6). Had the allowance started with a credit balance, say $200 left over from earlier estimates, the expense would have been only 584 − 200 = 384. The rule is the same in every case: expense = required balance − the balance already there, with a debit balance counted as a negative. After e6, net receivables are 7,380 − 584 = 6,796.

scenes.head: The adjustment can also run the other way.

segs.say: The adjustment can also run the other way. If fewer customers default than expected, the allowance may already hold more than the aging requires; the entry then debits Allowance for Doubtful Accounts and credits Bad Debt Expense for the excess, reducing the year’s expense.

scenes.head: The income statement approach would have given a different answer.

segs.say: The income statement approach would have given a different answer. Suppose Lantern’s accountant had expected losses of 2% of credit sales: the expense would be 0.02 × 59,920 = 1,198.40, and the allowance would end the year at 1,198.40 − 820 = 378.40, about $206 less than the aging says the receivables actually held need. The percentage of sales is quick and keeps the expense in proportion to the year’s sales, but nothing in it tests whether the allowance left on the balance sheet is a sensible estimate. A business may use it for monthly estimates, but at the reporting date the allowance itself has to be supported.

scenes.head: Expected credit losses: CECL (ASC 326) and IFRS 9

segs.say: Expected credit losses: CECL (ASC 326) and IFRS 9. US GAAP measures trade receivables under the current expected credit loss (CECL) model of ASC 326-20, introduced by ASU 2016-13 and in force, after the deferral in ASU 2019-10, for private companies such as Lantern for fiscal years beginning after 15 December 2022 (SEC filers other than smaller reporting companies applied it to fiscal years beginning after 15 December 2019). The allowance is a valuation account deducted from the receivables to present “the net amount expected to be collected” (ASC 326-20-30-1). It must reflect losses expected over the receivables’ contractual term, estimated from historical experience adjusted for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts, and assessed on a pool basis for receivables with similar risk. ASC 326-20-30-3 accepts several methods, including “methods that utilize an aging schedule”. ASU 2025-05 (July 2025, effective for annual periods beginning after 15 December 2025) adds a practical expedient for current receivables arising under ASC 606: an entity may assume that conditions at the balance sheet date do not change over the receivables’ remaining life, and a private company that does so may also take account of cash collected after the year end.

scenes.head: IFRS 9 reaches a similar place by a different route: for trade receivables without a significant financing component, the loss allowance is always…

segs.say: IFRS 9 reaches a similar place by a different route: for trade receivables without a significant financing component, the loss allowance is always measured at lifetime expected credit losses (IFRS 9, paragraph 5.5.15), often using a provision matrix much like an aging schedule. Under either framework the allowance is not zero just because no customer has yet defaulted: some loss is expected on almost any pool of receivables. The older incurred-loss rules, which this course doesn’t use, recorded a loss only once it was probable that it had already happened. For short trade receivables the two models often give similar numbers; the difference shows most in long-term loans, which are a subject for later courses.

scenes.head: A note receivable is a written promise by a customer or borrower to pay a stated sum on a stated date, usually with interest.

segs.say: A note receivable is a written promise by a customer or borrower to pay a stated sum on a stated date, usually with interest. Businesses take notes for large sales on longer terms, for loans to suppliers or staff, and sometimes in place of an overdue invoice, because a signed note is easier to enforce and earns interest. Interest is calculated as for a loan, I = P × r × t, and accrued at each period end as accrued revenue. A note due within a year of the balance sheet date is a current asset; a longer one is noncurrent. If the maker fails to pay at maturity (a dishonoured note), the holder usually transfers the principal and interest due back into Accounts Receivable and pursues it, or writes it off against the allowance.
Tarnside Joinery (fictional) takes a $6,000, six-month, 8% note in place of an overdue invoice

scenes.head: On the other side of the balance sheet, accounts payable (trade payables under IFRS) are amounts owed to suppliers for goods and services bought on…

segs.say: On the other side of the balance sheet, accounts payable (trade payables under IFRS) are amounts owed to suppliers for goods and services bought on credit. They are recorded when the goods or services are received, at the amount on the invoice, and removed when the supplier is paid. Lantern’s payables come from three sources: the beans bought from Kilnworth Roasting, supplies for events and workshops, and December’s utilities bill.

scenes.head: An accrued liability is the balance sheet side of an accrued expense: a cost incurred but not yet paid, for which no supplier’s invoice may yet exist.

segs.say: An accrued liability is the balance sheet side of an accrued expense: a cost incurred but not yet paid, for which no supplier’s invoice may yet exist. Wages earned in the last days of a period, interest building up on a loan, and utilities used but not yet billed are the usual examples. They are recorded by adjusting entries, as in F01. Some companies show them as a single line, “accrued liabilities”; Lantern shows Wages Payable and Interest Payable separately.

scenes.head: Two other current liabilities complete the list.

segs.say: Two other current liabilities complete the list. Unearned revenue is cash received for goods or services not yet delivered, called a contract liability in ASC 606 and IFRS 15; the revenue recognition lesson explains how it arises. It will be settled by delivering the service, not by paying cash. Income taxes payable is the tax owed for the period less the estimated payments already made. Lantern’s tax for the year is $9,129, 25% of its income before tax of $36,516; it paid $6,000 during the year, so $3,129 is still owed at 31 December.
Lantern Coffee Co.: current liabilities at 31 December 2026 and where each comes from (fictional)

scenes.head: The table shows why “current liabilities” is not the same as “cash Lantern must pay”.

segs.say: The table shows why “current liabilities” is not the same as “cash Lantern must pay”. Of the $26,289, the $6,100 of unearned revenue will be settled by serving customers. The current portion of the van note is the part of a long-term loan due within the next year; the next lesson explains how it is separated from the rest of the note. Every other line will take cash within the next five months.

scenes.head: When a supplier offers terms such as 2/10, n/30, the buyer chooses between paying 98% of the invoice on day 10 and 100% on day 30.

segs.say: When a supplier offers terms such as 2/10, n/30, the buyer chooses between paying 98% of the invoice on day 10 and 100% on day 30. Skipping the discount is in effect borrowing 98% of the invoice for 20 days and paying 2% for the privilege. The cost of that borrowing, at a simple annual rate, is 2/98 × 365/20 ≈ 37.2%, far above what most businesses pay a bank. That is why well-run businesses take such discounts whenever they have the cash, and why a business that stops taking them is often short of cash. How a discount taken is recorded in the inventory accounts is covered in the inventory lesson.

scenes.head: Accounts receivable roll-forward

segs.say: Accounts receivable roll-forward: AR_(end) = AR_(beg) + Credit sales − Collections − Write-offs.
AR_(beg), AR_(end): Accounts receivable at the start and end of the period (gross, before the allowance) ($).
Credit sales: Sales invoiced to customers on credit during the period ($).
Collections: Cash received from customers against their accounts ($).
Write-offs: Customer balances removed as uncollectible during the period ($).
Lantern, 2026: 0 + 59,920 − 51,720 − 820 = 7,380. A reinstated recovery adds back to receivables and is then collected.

scenes.head: Allowance required by an aging of receivables

segs.say: Allowance required by an aging of receivables: Required allowance = Σᵢ Bᵢ × rᵢ.
Bᵢ: Receivables in age band i (for example, not yet due, 31–60 days, over 60 days) ($).
rᵢ: Expected loss rate for band i, as a decimal; higher for older bands.
Σᵢ: Sum over all the age bands.
It assumes this: The rates reflect past losses adjusted for current conditions and reasonable forecasts.

scenes.head: Bad debt expense under the balance sheet approach

segs.say: Bad debt expense under the balance sheet approach: Bad debt expense = Required allowance − Unadjusted allowance.
Required allowance: The credit balance the allowance must have after adjustment (from the aging or a percentage of receivables) ($).
Unadjusted allowance: The allowance’s balance before the adjustment: positive if a credit balance, negative if a debit balance ($).
A debit balance adds to the expense: Lantern’s is 584 − (−820) = 1,404.

scenes.head: Bad debt expense under the income statement approach

segs.say: Bad debt expense under the income statement approach: Bad debt expense = p × Credit sales.
p: Expected loss rate on credit sales, as a decimal.
Credit sales: Sales on credit for the period (cash and card sales carry no credit risk) ($).
The allowance after adjustment is whatever results: unadjusted balance plus the expense.

scenes.head: Net receivables (net realisable value of receivables)

segs.say: Net receivables (net realisable value of receivables): Net receivables = Accounts receivable − Allowance for doubtful accounts.
Accounts receivable: Gross amount customers owe at the balance sheet date ($).
Allowance for doubtful accounts: Credit balance of the allowance after adjustment ($).
Lantern: 7,380 − 584 = 6,796, the amount it expects to collect.

scenes.head: Interest on a note for part of a year

segs.say: Interest on a note for part of a year: I = P × r × t.
I: Interest earned (or owed) for the period ($).
P: Principal of the note ($).
r: Annual interest rate, as a decimal.
t: Time in years: months outstanding ÷ 12 (years).

scenes.head: Annualised cost of skipping a cash discount

segs.say: Annualised cost of skipping a cash discount: Cost = d/(1 − d) × 365/(n − p).
d: Discount for early payment, as a decimal (2% = 0.02).
n: Days until the full amount is due (30 in 2/10, n/30) (days).
p: Last day of the discount period (10 in 2/10, n/30) (days).
It assumes this: A simple (not compounded) annual rate; the buyer would otherwise pay on the last day of each period.
Compounding gives a higher effective annual rate: (1/0.98)^(365/20) − 1 ≈ 44.6% for 2/10, n/30.

chapters.title: Example: An aging for an office-furniture supplier

scenes.head: An aging for an office-furniture supplier

segs.say: Fernbrook Office Furniture, a fictional supplier to offices and schools, ages its receivables at 31 December as shown. Before adjustment its allowance for doubtful accounts has a credit balance of $1,140. Find the allowance required, the bad debt expense, the adjusting entry and net receivables.

scenes.head: An aging for an office-furniture supplier

segs.say: Step 2. Required allowance: 480 + 500 + 930 + 1,650 = 3,560.

Step 3. The allowance already has a credit balance of 1,140, so only the difference is new expense: 3,560 − 1,140 = 2,420. Entry: debit Bad Debt Expense 2,420; credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 2,420.
Step 4. Net receivables: 70,000 − 3,560 = 66,440.

scenes.head: An aging for an office-furniture supplier

segs.say: Required allowance $3,560; bad debt expense $2,420 (debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts); net receivables $66,440.
Almost half the allowance comes from the $3,300 more than 60 days overdue, less than 5% of the receivables. Chasing the oldest balances is where Fernbrook’s credit controller can save the most.

chapters.title: Example: A year in the allowance account

scenes.head: A year in the allowance account

segs.say: Corrib Outdoor Clothing, a fictional brand that sells jackets and boots to independent shops on 60-day terms, starts 2026 with an allowance credit balance of $9,000. During the year it makes credit sales of $760,000 and writes off three shops’ balances totalling $11,600. In October a shop written off in 2025 pays $1,100. At 31 December receivables are $240,000, aged as in the table. Record the recovery, find the bad debt expense and net receivables, and compare the result with a policy of 1.5% of credit sales.

scenes.head: A year in the allowance account

segs.say: Step 1. The recovery is two entries: reinstate $1,100 (debit Accounts Receivable, credit the allowance), then record the cash (debit Cash, credit Accounts Receivable). The reinstatement puts the $1,100 back into the allowance, because the loss charged in 2025 turned out not to have happened.
Step 2. Unadjusted allowance: 9,000 − 11,600 + 1,100 = −1,500, a debit balance of 1,500. The year’s write-offs were larger than the opening allowance plus the recovery.
Step 3. Required allowance from the aging: 1,680 + 1,680 + 2,520 + 4,500 = 10,380.
Step 5. The sales-based policy would charge 0.015 × 760,000 = 11,400 and leave an allowance of 11,400 − 1,500 = 9,900, which is 480 short of what the aging says the year-end receivables need.

scenes.head: A year in the allowance account

segs.say: Bad debt expense $11,880; allowance $10,380; net receivables $229,620. The 1.5% policy would have charged $11,400 and left the allowance $480 too small.

The debit balance is a warning sign: the year’s write-offs, on 2025’s sales and on 2026’s, outran the $9,000 the allowance started with. If that happens year after year, Corrib’s loss rates are too low, and its profits are overstated in the years the sales are made.

chapters.title: Example: Should Lantern take Kilnworth’s discount?

scenes.head: Should Lantern take Kilnworth’s discount?

segs.say: Suppose Kilnworth Roasting offered Lantern terms of 2/10, n/30 instead of plain 30-day terms. Lantern’s bean purchases averaged $5,860 a month in 2026 ($58,600 over ten months), and it holds $42,940 in cash. Should Ana pay on day 10?

scenes.head: Should Lantern take Kilnworth’s discount?

segs.say: Step 1. The discount on a typical month: 0.02 × 5,860 = 117.20. Paying on day 10 costs 5,860 − 117.20 = 5,742.80; waiting costs 5,860 on day 30.
Step 2. Waiting is like borrowing 5,742.80 for 20 days at a cost of 117.20: 117.20 ÷ 5,742.80 ≈ 2.04% for 20 days, which is 2/98.
Step 3. Annualise (discount-cost formula): 2/98 × 365/20 ≈ 37.2% a year at a simple rate, about 44.6% compounded.

Step 4. Lantern’s cash earns far less than that, and even a bank overdraft would cost much less, so taking the discount is the better use of cash. Over a year of similar purchases it saves about 12 × 117.20 = 1,406.40.

scenes.head: Should Lantern take Kilnworth’s discount?

segs.say: Yes: skipping the discount costs the equivalent of about 37% a year. Paying on day 10 saves about $117 a month, roughly $1,406 a year.

Credit terms are a source of finance with a price. Free 30-day credit is worth using in full; credit that costs 2% for 20 days is not. A business that can’t afford the discount is borrowing at 37%, which is worth telling its bank.

scenes.head: Aging of receivables and the year-end adjustment

segs.say: The defaults are Lantern’s aging and its allowance’s debit balance of $820 before adjustment. Change the amounts and loss rates, or the starting balance, and watch the required allowance, the bad debt expense and net receivables. Try a credit balance larger than the requirement: the entry then reduces the allowance. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Work through Lantern’s receivables entries for the year: the invoices (y8), the collections (y9), the Quayline write-off (y10) and the year-end estimate (e6). For each, choose the accounts, the direction and side, the amount and the statements affected. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “A write-off is when the bad debt expense is recorded.”

segs.say: “A write-off is when the bad debt expense is recorded.”. Under the allowance method the expense is recorded at the period end, when the loss is estimated. The write-off moves a named customer’s balance out of receivables and out of the allowance; it changes neither the expense nor, when the allowance is adequate, net receivables.

scenes.head: “Bad debt expense is the allowance figure from the aging.”

segs.say: “Bad debt expense is the allowance figure from the aging.”. The aging gives the balance the allowance must end with. The expense is that balance minus what is already in the account. Lantern’s aging says $584, but its expense is $1,404, because the account started at a debit of $820.

scenes.head: “A debit balance in the allowance is subtracted.”

segs.say: “A debit balance in the allowance is subtracted.”. A debit balance means losses have already outrun the allowance. The adjustment has to fill that hole before building the new balance, so a debit balance is added: 584 + 820. Subtract only a credit balance.

scenes.head: “The percentage of sales gives the allowance.”

segs.say: “The percentage of sales gives the allowance.”. Under the income statement approach the percentage of sales gives the expense; the allowance is what is left after adding it to the unadjusted balance. Mixing the two approaches (taking a percentage of sales as the required balance) is a common slip.

scenes.head: “Unearned revenue will be paid out in cash.”

segs.say: “Unearned revenue will be paid out in cash.”. Unearned revenue is a liability because Lantern owes a service. It is settled by delivering the events, workshop and coffee, and turns into revenue as it does. Treating it as a cash outflow overstates the cash a business needs.

scenes.head: In businesses that sell on credit, the aging is a working document long before it becomes an adjusting entry.

segs.say: In businesses that sell on credit, the aging is a working document long before it becomes an adjusting entry. A credit controller reviews it every week: invoices just past due get a reminder, older ones a telephone call, and a customer whose balance keeps sliding into the older bands may be put on stop or asked for a deposit before the next order. New customers are given a credit limit after a check of their references or credit file. The loss rates in the year-end estimate are only as good as this follow-up, which is why auditors compare last year’s allowance with what was actually lost and test the aging against the payments received after the year end.

scenes.head: Lantern’s own aging points to two actions.

segs.say: Lantern’s own aging points to two actions. The $820 more than 60 days overdue carries a 40% loss rate; a personal call from Ana is worth more than another emailed reminder. And Quayline’s failure suggests a policy for one-off event agencies: a deposit of a third or a half when the booking is made, as Harbor Tech already pays. Deposits turn a credit risk into unearned revenue, a liability Lantern settles by doing the work it is good at.

scenes.head: Payables are a question of timing and cash.

segs.say: Payables are a question of timing and cash. Of Lantern’s $26,289 of current liabilities, $6,100 will be settled by serving customers; the other $20,189 needs cash over the next five months, from accounts payable and wages in January to the tax payment and the first van instalment on 1 June. Against that Lantern holds $42,940 in the bank and expects $6,796 from its catering clients, so it can pay every bill on time and take any discount offered. Measures that turn these balances into collection and payment periods, such as days sales outstanding, belong to F03.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Accounts receivable are amounts customers owe on credit terms; the roll-forward is beginning balance + credit sales − collections − write-offs (Lantern: 0 + 59,920 − 51,720 − 820 = $7,380).
The allowance method records expected losses as bad debt expense in the period of the sale and holds them in a contra-asset; write-offs are charged against the allowance with no new expense.
The direct write-off method delays the expense and overstates receivables, so US GAAP and IFRS allow it only for immaterial amounts; tax deductions, by contrast, follow write-offs.
Under the balance sheet approach, expense = required allowance − unadjusted balance (a debit balance adds): Lantern’s aging requires $584, so e6 is 584 + 820 = $1,404 and net receivables are $6,796.
CECL (ASC 326-20) and IFRS 9 measure the allowance as expected credit losses using history, current conditions and forecasts; an aging schedule or provision matrix is an accepted method.
Notes receivable earn interest, I = P × r × t, accrued at each period end and collected at maturity.

Current liabilities include accounts payable, accrued liabilities, unearned revenue, income taxes payable and the current portion of long-term debt: $26,289 for Lantern, of which $6,100 is settled by service rather than cash.
Skipping a 2/10, n/30 discount costs about 37% a year at a simple rate, so a business with cash should take it.
